result.markdown: --- title: "Session 5 — Choosing, Comparing and Reporting" subtitle: "Ordinal vs multinomial · probability plots · classification accuracy · tables · checklist · Lab 5" author: "Community Medicine Workshop" format: revealjs: theme: serif css: [../assets/slide_deck.css, assets/workshop.css, assets/quiz.css] include-after-body: assets/quiz-include.html embed-resources: true slide-number: true navigation-mode: linear code-copy: true center: false transition: fade width: 1280 height: 720 fig-align: center html-math-method: plain execute: echo: true warning: false message: false fig-width: 9 fig-height: 4.6 fig-dpi: 100 --- ## Where we are ::: {.incremental} - Sessions 1-4: ordered and nominal outcomes, the assumption, the models - Today: **choose** between them, **show** the results, **report** - By the end you can: - justify **ordinal vs multinomial** - plot **predicted probabilities** - judge a model without relying on **accuracy** - write the **methods and results** ::: # Topic 1 — Ordinal or multinomial? {background-color="#2C3E50"} ## A decision | Question | Answer | Model | |---|---|---| | Is there a **meaningful order**? | No | **Multinomial** logistic | | | Yes | **Ordinal** logistic (proportional odds) | | Does **proportional odds** hold (Brant, cut-point ORs)? | Yes | one OR per predictor | | | One or a few predictors fail | **Partial** proportional odds | | | Many fail | **Multinomial** | ## The same data, two models ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} a_ord <- MASS::polr(anaemia ~ wealth + tribal, data = mat, Hess = TRUE) a_mn <- nnet::multinom(factor(anaemia, ordered = FALSE) ~ wealth + tribal, data = mat, trace = FALSE) c(ordinal = AIC(a_ord), multinomial = AIC(a_mn)) |> round(0) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` ordinal multinomial 3200 3170 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.key} The multinomial model has the **lower AIC** because it frees the tribal effect at each cut-point; it also needs **many more parameters** (9 vs 5). When proportional odds **holds**, the ordinal model is simpler and **more powerful**. When it fails and cannot be relaxed, **multinomial is the safe fallback**. ::: # Topic 2 — Showing results {background-color="#2C3E50"} ## Probabilities against a predictor ::: {.cell output-location='slide'} ```{.r .cell-code} m_ord <- MASS::polr(anaemia ~ wealth + education + bmi + anc_visits + parity + age + tribal + residence, data = mat, Hess = TRUE) nd <- data.frame(wealth = 1:5, education = factor("Primary", levels = levels(mat$education)), bmi = 20.5, anc_visits = 3, parity = 2, age = 27, tribal = factor("No", levels = c("No", "Yes")), residence = factor("Rural", levels = c("Urban", "Rural"))) cbind(wealth = 1:5, as.data.frame(predict(m_ord, newdata = nd, type = "probs"))) |> pivot_longer(-wealth, names_to = "anaemia", values_to = "probability") |> mutate(anaemia = factor(anaemia, levels = levels(mat$anaemia))) |> ggplot(aes(wealth, probability, colour = anaemia)) + geom_line(linewidth = 1.2) + labs(x = "Wealth quintile", y = "Predicted probability", colour = NULL) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](s5_choosing_reporting_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-3-1.png){width=900} ::: ::: The same idea for the nominal outcome: predicted probabilities of each **delivery place** across wealth show **home falling and private rising**. ## Accuracy is a weak summary ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} mat$delivery <- relevel(mat$delivery, ref = "Home") mn <- nnet::multinom(delivery ~ wealth + education + anc_visits + residence + tribal, data = mat, trace = FALSE) c(model = mean(predict(mn) == mat$delivery), always_most_common = max(prop.table(table(mat$delivery)))) |> round(2) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` model always_most_common 0.48 0.32 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.warn} The model is right about **48%** of the time vs **32%** for always guessing the most common place. Covariates **shift probabilities** but **cannot predict an individual's choice**; accuracy ignores the probabilities. Use **predicted probabilities**, **AIC** or **log-likelihood**, and, if prediction is the aim, **calibration** and **proper scoring rules**. ::: # Topic 3 — Reporting {background-color="#2C3E50"} ## Wording ::: {.good} **Ordinal:** "In a proportional-odds model adjusted for education, BMI, antenatal visits, parity, age, tribal group and residence, each higher wealth quintile was associated with **24% lower odds** of being in a worse anaemia category (OR 0.76, 95% CI ...). The assumption held for all predictors except tribal group, so its effect is reported separately at each cut-point." ::: ::: {.good} **Multinomial:** "Compared with home delivery, each wealth quintile increased the **relative risk** of delivering in a private hospital 2.8-fold (RRR 2.76, 95% CI ...)." ::: ## Reporting checklist ::: {.incremental} 1. **Outcome** categories, order, **counts**; **reference** category (nominal) 2. **Model** and **why** (ordered or not); **software** (`MASS`, `nnet`, `ordinal`) 3. **Odds ratios** (ordinal) or **relative risk ratios** (multinomial) with **95% CI**; adjustment set 4. **Assumption check** (Brant, cut-specific ORs) and what you did 5. **Predicted probabilities** for key profiles 6. **Limitations**: sparse categories, many parameters, association not cause, self-reported outcomes ::: ## 🔧 Switch to R — Lab 5 {.lab-slide background-color="#1565c0"} ::: {.lab-box} **File:** `ordinal-workshop/labs/lab5_report.R` - ordinal vs multinomial fitted to the same ordered outcome - probability tables and a plot - accuracy against guessing; a publication table ::: **Time:** 30 minutes · answer the Q questions in the comments ## Self-check quiz (1/5) {.smaller} ::: {.quiz-q data-qid="s5q1" data-type="mcq" data-hash="tkkmp0.4t433a" data-show="UHJvcG9ydGlvbmFsIG9kZHMgZmFpbHMgZm9yIG1hbnkgcHJlZGljdG9ycyBhbmQgY2Fubm90 IGJlIHJlbGF4ZWQ=" data-explain="TXVsdGlub21pYWwgbWFrZXMgbm8gb3JkZXJpbmcgYXNzdW1wdGlvbiwgc28gaXQgaXMgdGhl IGZhbGxiYWNrIHdoZW4gcHJvcG9ydGlvbmFsIG9kZHMgY2xlYXJseSBmYWlscy4gSXQgdXNl cyBtb3JlIHBhcmFtZXRlcnMgYW5kIHNvIG5lZWRzIGEgbGFyZ2VyIHNhbXBsZS4="} When is the multinomial model a good choice for an ordered outcome? - The sample of women is very small for a model with many parameters - All the predictors in the model are binary variables only - Proportional odds fails for many predictors and cannot be relaxed - The outcome has three ordered categories in the data set ::: ## Self-check quiz (2/5) {.smaller} ::: {.quiz-q data-qid="s5q2" data-type="mcq" data-hash="tkkzxo.4t4hkm" data-show="Q292YXJpYXRlcyBzaGlmdCBwcm9iYWJpbGl0aWVzLCBidXQgYWNjdXJhY3kgaXMgYSB3ZWFr IHN1bW1hcnk=" data-explain="RXZlbiBhIHVzZWZ1bCBtb2RlbCBtYXkgcHJlZGljdCBhbiBpbmRpdmlkdWFsJ3MgY2F0ZWdv cnkgcG9vcmx5LiBBY2N1cmFjeSBpZ25vcmVzIHRoZSBwcmVkaWN0ZWQgcHJvYmFiaWxpdGll cywgc28ganVkZ2UgdGhlIG1vZGVsIGJ5IHByb2JhYmlsaXRpZXMsIGxpa2VsaWhvb2QgYW5k IGNhbGlicmF0aW9uLg=="} The multinomial model classifies 48% of women correctly and always guessing the most common place gives 32%. What is the best conclusion? - The model is excellent, since it beats guessing the most common place - Covariates shift probabilities, but accuracy is a weak summary - The model has failed and should be rejected for this use - The two numbers cannot be compared with each other in any way ::: ## Self-check quiz (3/5) {.smaller} ::: {.quiz-q data-qid="s5q3" data-type="mcq" data-hash="tkld6e.4t4w20" data-show="VGhleSBzaG93IGhvdyBlYWNoIGNhdGVnb3J5J3MgcHJvYmFiaWxpdHkgY2hhbmdlcyB3aXRo IGl0" data-explain="VGhlIHBsb3Qgc2hvd3Mgd2hhdCB0aGUgbW9kZWwgaW1wbGllcyBmb3IgcmVhZGVycyBvbiB0 aGUgcHJvYmFiaWxpdHkgc2NhbGU6IGZvciBleGFtcGxlIGhvbWUgZGVsaXZlcmllcyBmYWxs aW5nIGFuZCBwcml2YXRlIHJpc2luZy4="} Why plot predicted probabilities against a predictor such as wealth? - They give the p-value of the Brant test for the predictor shown - They replace the need for odds ratios in any paper that is written - They show how each category's probability changes with it - They prove that the effect of the predictor is a causal one ::: ## Self-check quiz (4/5) {.smaller} ::: {.quiz-q data-qid="s5q4" data-type="mcq" data-hash="tklqf4.4t5aje" data-show="RWFjaCBoaWdoZXIgcXVpbnRpbGUgd2VudCB3aXRoIDI0JSBsb3dlciBvZGRzIG9mIGEgd29y c2UgY2F0ZWdvcnkgKE9SIDAuNzYp" data-explain="U3RhdGUgdGhlIE9SIGZvciBhIGhpZ2hlciBjYXRlZ29yeSB3aXRoIGl0cyBDSSBhbmQgdGhl IGFkanVzdG1lbnQuIEF2b2lkIHRyZWF0aW5nIGNhdGVnb3JpZXMgYXMgbnVtYmVycyBvciBn aXZpbmcgb25seSBhIHAtdmFsdWUu"} Which sentence is the best way to report an ordinal result when the assumption holds? - Each higher quintile lowers the anaemia grade by 0.76 of one whole category - Wealthy women have 76% of the anaemia that is found in poor women - Wealth had a significant effect on anaemia because the p-value was small - Each higher quintile went with 24% lower odds of a worse category (OR 0.76) ::: ## Self-check quiz (5/5) {.smaller} ::: {.quiz-q data-qid="s5q5" data-type="mcq" data-hash="tkm3nq.4t5p0o" data-show="U3BhcnNlIGNhdGVnb3JpZXMsIG1hbnkgcGFyYW1ldGVycywgYW5kIGFzc29jaWF0aW9uIG5v dCBiZWluZyBjYXVzZQ==" data-explain="U21hbGwgY2F0ZWdvcmllcyBhbmQgbWFueSBwYXJhbWV0ZXJzIGRlc3RhYmlsaXNlIGVzdGlt YXRlcywgYW5kIGFuIG9ic2VydmF0aW9uYWwgZGVzaWduIHN1cHBvcnRzIGFzc29jaWF0aW9u IG9ubHku"} What belongs in the limitations of a categorical-outcome analysis? - Sparse categories, many parameters, and association not being cause - The fact that the outcome has more than two categories to model - That odds ratios cannot be reported when there are many categories - That the software used for the analysis was written in the R language ::: ## Score and take-home **Your score: ** ::: {.incremental} - Ordered and the assumption holds: **ordinal**; fails for one or two: **partial**; many or no order: **multinomial** - Show **predicted probabilities** and plots, not only odds ratios - Do not judge by **classification accuracy** - Report **categories, reference, model, ORs/RRRs with CI, assumption check, limitations** ::: **Next:** The cheat sheet and the Dungeons & Dataframes ordinal and nominal world (coming)

<script>
  // htmlwidgets need to know to resize themselves when slides are shown/hidden.
  // Fire the "slideenter" event (handled by htmlwidgets.js) when the current
  // slide changes (different for each slide format).
  (function () {
    // dispatch for htmlwidgets
    function fireSlideEnter() {
      const event = window.document.createEvent("Event");
      event.initEvent("slideenter", true, true);
      window.document.dispatchEvent(event);
    }

    function fireSlideChanged(previousSlide, currentSlide) {
      fireSlideEnter();

      // dispatch for shiny
      if (window.jQuery) {
        if (previousSlide) {
          window.jQuery(previousSlide).trigger("hidden");
        }
        if (currentSlide) {
          window.jQuery(currentSlide).trigger("shown");
        }
      }
    }

    // hookup for slidy
    if (window.w3c_slidy) {
      window.w3c_slidy.add_observer(function (slide_num) {
        // slide_num starts at position 1
        fireSlideChanged(null, w3c_slidy.slides[slide_num - 1]);
      });
    }

  })();
</script>
